title.en: Accuracy, precision and kinds of errors

hook.en: Four friends throw darts. One hits the bull every time; one hits the same wrong spot every time; one scatters darts all round the bull; one scatters them all over the board. Measurements behave the same way.

objectives.en: Name systematic, random and gross errors
Use least count and zero error correctly

narration.en: Four friends throw darts. One hits the bull every time; one hits the same wrong spot every time; one scatters darts all round the bull; one scatters them all over the board. Measurements behave the same way.

body.en: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value. Precision is how closely repeated measurements agree, and how fine a step (the least count) the instrument can show. A metre scale reads to 1 mm, a vernier calliper to 0.1 mm and a screw gauge to 0.01 mm. Good measurements are both accurate and precise.

points.en: Accuracy: closeness to the true value
Precision: closeness of readings to each other

title.en: Accuracy and precision on a target

narration.en: Each dot is one reading. Move the offset to add a systematic error. Increase the scatter to add random error. Try to make readings that are precise but not accurate.

caption.en: Each dot is one reading. The offset moves the centre of the readings away from the true value (a systematic error); the scatter spreads them out (random error). Press New readings for another set.

tryThis.en: Make the readings precise but not accurate.
Make them accurate on average but not precise.
Which slider does averaging many readings help with?

body.en: Systematic errors push every reading the same way: a zero error, a wrongly calibrated scale, parallax from always looking at an angle, a thermometer that is not in thermal contact. They are found and removed by correction, not by averaging. Random errors come from small unpredictable changes and scatter readings both ways; averaging many readings reduces them. Gross errors are mistakes (a misread scale, a wrong entry) and the readings are discarded.

points.en: Random: both directions; average many readings
Least count error: half the least count or one least count

title.en: Zero error of a screw gauge

say.en: Close the jaws. If the zero of the circular scale is below the reference line, every reading is too large.
Zero error is plus 4 times the least count, 0.04 millimetre. Subtract it from every reading.

aim.en: To use precise instruments (screw gauge, vernier) and see how each measurement's least count limits the result.

narration.en: Optional lab: the Young's modulus bench uses a screw gauge for the wire and a vernier for the extension, the two most precise readings of school physics.

problem.en: A vernier calliper has 20 vernier divisions equal to 19 main-scale divisions of 1 mm. With the jaws closed, the vernier zero is to the right of the main zero and the 5th vernier line coincides. A rod gives main-scale reading 23 mm and the 12th vernier line coincides. Find the corrected length.

body.en: Ask: does the error always push the same way? If yes, it is systematic: find it and correct it. If no, it is random: take many readings and average.

mnemonic.en: Same way: correct. Both ways: average.

points.en: Accuracy: close to the true value; precision: close to each other and to a fine least count.
Systematic errors are corrected; random errors are reduced by averaging; gross errors are discarded.
Correct reading = observed − zero error (with its sign).

homework.en: A screw gauge has a least count of 0.01 mm and a zero error of −0.03 mm. A wire reads 1.47 mm. Find the true diameter. (Answer: 1.50 mm)
